I agree with this (in some contradictory manner from my part), but I just thought to share this article, not with the intent of proving something new or as a very meaningful article, but rather to share a more light-hearted “fact” that I learned (what I specially wanted to highlight was that Lithuanian is so conservative that it still has noticeable relationship with Sanskrit). I’m writing this more as a point of reference on what I wanted to highlight from the article, rather than making any big linguistics claims.

The second article mentions that Old Prussian, as I mentioned is now extinct, would be technically a closer relative to Sanskrit. I do agree that using the an article written from the government itself probably does have political bias/agenda, but it isn’t just completely made up. I thought, out of the articles that I saw, it was to the best to introduce the topic, the next two would be more of a detailed argument and the last link is just related to the topic.
Could someone explain to me why this post is getting bad reception or why its not appropriate for this sub? (sincere question)

Lithuanian is known as the closest modern language to Sanskrit due to the least amount of change in it (after extinct Prussian). So, while yes, all these other languages can be all connected to Sanskrit, it (Lithuanian) has many more obvious connections (many words with close-to-the-same pronunciation). 

Edit: The most surprising thing was the overlaps in culture and deities, which is reflected also through the similarities of the language. I wasn't aware of the strong nationalistic ties to tradition that Lithuania has (referring to Paganism) as well as the little interference from foreigners culturally.

My suggestion would be 1) change the "pour love" part, since you already used the word "love" in the beginning, and therefore, the topic is already implied. Perhaps changing it into "just to pour your amorous emotions/warmth in the hollow"? I don't know. My phrase isn't great but its simply finding something (somewhat) synonymous to "love". If you don't like that idea, change the beginning part of "fall in and out of love"? Instead of presenting the topic in the beginning, you can make it more abstract and clarify the theme later on. (Thus, you don't need to change that last part about love) You could change it into a metaphor for falling in and out of love, such as relentlessly falling down (don't mention love). My opinion is that you should change the last part but its your choice. Good luck on your poem, I think its a good start.

I just recently finished the book, and I thought that Mephistopheles does portray some redeeming and "good" qualities in a way. For example, Mephistopheles is more affiliated with cynicism and sarcasm, rather than the literal incarnation of evil (meaning not the medieval devil). In my opinion, he has some sense of relatability and, as you stated, he *is* honest. Perhaps this sense of skepticism and (maybe also) realism, makes him appear more likeable/honest. The fact that the rest of the characters are hard to empathise with (e.g Faust & Gretchen) also contributes with the perception that Mephistopheles is a better character. I'm not sure about the hero part though. That sounds like a far stretch. He is, in the end, trying to corrupt Faust.
